references.text: In Matthew's parallel account, those standing around say to Peter that his dialect reveals him as a Galilean: 'Truly, you also are one of them, for your speech gives you away' ([ref:Matt 26:73|Matthew 26:73]). This corresponds to the content of the accusation in Luke 22:59, where another person insists that Peter was with Jesus because he is a Galilean.

Mark's parallel account of Peter's third denial, where those standing around say: 'Truly you are one of them, for you also are a Galilean' ([ref:Mark 14:70|Mark 14:70]). The same point of accusation as in Luke: Peter's Galilean background links him to Jesus.

In John's account, it is a relative of Malchus who recognizes Peter and says: 'Did I not see you in the garden with him?' ([ref:Joh 18:26-27|John 18:26-27]). This is the third accusation situation that results in Peter's denial, parallel to Luke 22:59.

The context for Peter's denial begins with Peter following Jesus at a distance to the high priest's courtyard ([ref:Luk 22:54|Luke 22:54]). This explains why Peter found himself in the situation where he was recognized and accused.

Jesus' prediction that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed ([ref:Luk 22:34|Luke 22:34]). This third accusation situation in verse 59 is the final link in the fulfillment of Jesus' prophecy.

On the day of Pentecost, the listeners notice that the disciples are Galileans: 'Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?' ([ref:Apg 2:7|Acts 2:7]). The disciples' Galilean origin was clearly recognizable to people in Jerusalem, which supports that Peter's background could easily reveal his connection to Jesus.
